title: No perspiration, no exaltation

stances.claim: Success -- economic, professional, or spiritual -- is built on pain and sacrifice; 'no perspiration, no exaltation.'

CJ's own hardscrabble youth -- hawking newspapers, shining shoes, selling textbooks, and building the family house in Marulas with his own hands -- taught him 'the value of hard work and steely determination to succeed.'

stances.claim: Jensen Huang's rise to Nvidia and over $100 billion net worth, despite Taiwan-immigrant disadvantage and prejudice, exemplifies the same pattern -- as does his message to the Stanford graduating class.

Lance Gokongwei's phenomenal rise -- Wharton summa cum laude graduate who nonetheless began as a Jack-and-Jill management trainee selling to sari-sari stores -- shows that even heirs apparent must undergo pain and embarrassment from the bottom.

When suffering is undergone with love, it becomes 'sacrifice' -- the Christian transformation that gives pain its triumphal purpose; this is illustrated by Christ on the cross, by a mother giving birth, and by a student burning the midnight oil.

one_paragraph_summary: At a private family dinner honoring his three grandchildren -- Andrea, Rafa, and Victoria -- for scholarships granted by top US universities (the subject of his previous column), CJ delivered as pater de familia a special message and now publishes an abbreviated version 'easy to remember': 'No pain, no gain. No sacrifice, no victory. No perspiration, no exaltation.' He amplifies the message with four stories. First, his own impoverished youth -- hawking newspapers, shining shoes in grade school and high school, and selling textbooks to classmates in college -- and, during law school, literally building with his brother Nardo, his orphaned half-uncle Frankie Villasenor, and a master carpenter a two-story house in Marulas, Polo, Bulacan (now Valenzuela City). He learned to draft architectural plans, slept in a tent at the site to fend off rain, mosquitoes, and robbers, and acquired the hands-on skills of carpenter, plumber, electrician, cement mixer, concrete-hollow-block maker, and peon. Second, the biography of Jensen Huang, who rose from a Taiwan-immigrant household in the US -- through hard manual labor and seething anti-Chinese prejudice -- to found Nvidia in 1993 and reach a net worth above $100 billion (Forbes, June 4, 2024); Huang told the Stanford graduating class (paraphrased): 'To succeed, you must endure pain and suffering first.' Third, the rise of Lance Gokongwei, a Wharton summa cum laude graduate who began as a management trainee 'selling Jack and Jill snacks to supermarkets, groceries, and sari-sari stores' with no privileges despite being heir apparent, and who inherited a $20-billion conglomerate at his father's 2019 death -- assuming leadership at 52. Fourth, the teaching of Our Lord Jesus, paraphrased: 'He who is worthy of me must take up his cross and follow me.' CJ closes by distinguishing 'pain and suffering' from 'pain and sacrifice' -- for Christians, suffering undergone with love becomes sacrifice, like a mother giving birth or a student burning the midnight oil. To his grandchildren: the scholarship 'is just the beginning' -- be ready to undergo pain and sacrifice 'for your education, for your career, for our family, for our country, and for our God.'
